hook: Sometimes you have no graph and no simple algebra, just a function you can evaluate, or a set of measurements. Then you test: plug in inputs closer and closer to the point, from both sides, and watch the outputs. A well-chosen table can reveal a limit in seconds, and a badly read one can mislead. This topic shows both.

options: When both one-sided limits exist and are equal
When the graph has no holes
prereq.why: Both sides must exist and agree.

prereq.q: Which inputs approach 4 from the left?
prereq.why: From the left means below 4, getting closer.

figure.caption: A table of values closing in on $x = 2$ from both sides, and the same points on a zoomed-in graph: the outputs settle on 0.25.

chain.cause: Choose inputs closer and closer to $a$ from the left, and from the right (never $a$ itself)
chain.effect: the outputs show each one-sided trend

chain.cause: Both sides settle on the same number
chain.effect: that number is a numerical estimate of the limit

chain.cause: The sides settle on different numbers, grow without bound, or keep jumping around
chain.effect: the table suggests the limit does not exist

chain.cause: A table checks only finitely many inputs
chain.effect: it suggests a limit but cannot prove it; confirm with a graph or algebra

ideas: To estimate $\lim_{x \to a} f(x)$, evaluate $f$ at inputs like $a - 0.1, a - 0.01, a - 0.001$ and $a + 0.001, a + 0.01, a + 0.1$.
Read each side separately, exactly as on a graph: the left-hand limit uses inputs below $a$, the right-hand limit inputs above $a$.
The estimate is the number the outputs approach, not the last value in the table. A value $f(a)$ in the table never decides the limit.
A table can mislead if it stops too early. If the values have not settled, test inputs even closer to $a$.

misconception.wrong: The limit is the table value at the input closest to $a$.
misconception.right: The limit is the number the values approach. The closest value, such as 27.009001, is only an approximation of the limit, 27.

summary: A table estimates a limit when it lists outputs for inputs closing in on $a$ from both sides. If both sides settle on the same number, that is the estimate; if they differ, grow without bound or never settle, the limit appears not to exist. A table suggests; it does not prove, so check closer inputs or use algebra when in doubt.
